text.content: 7: Future History n the twentieth century, humans first left the surface of Earth and took to the skies. They used aircraft to travel around the planet through its atmosphere, but soon, they left the Earth’s pull, using spacecraft to reach into orbit and then to the surface of Earth’s moon. Caught up in the excitement of a “space race”, dozens of unmanned probes were launched in efforts to learn about other planets in the solar system, revealing an enormous wealth of raw materials. They dug further, eventually mapping the moons of the outer planets. No one expected to uncover a secret that would change the course of human history.

After those heady early days, humans maintained only a small presence in space through orbital stations orbiting their home planet. Progress only resumed years later when humanity took another bold leap through space to Earth’s nearest planetary neighbor—Mars. Later expeditions included colonists who went to stay. These scientists, engineers, and laborers developed the terraforming technologies needed to undertake the long project of turning Mars into a second home for humanity. In search of new work and new opportunities, entire families left their home planet and committed to the effort. Although they hailed from separate places and cultures, here they lived side by side and became one people: Martians. The Martians needed a steady supply of raw materials unavailable on their new world, which meant regular ships traveling between Earth and Mars. Back on Earth, the cost of humanity’s long journey was finally coming due. For thousands of years, humans had extracted resources from the planet in ever-increasing amounts, and Earth’s exploding population had either disturbed or out-and-out replaced countless natural cycles and habitats. Worse, little had been done to remediate the effects of technological and industrial development, polluting much of the planet and leaving some parts nearly uninhabitable. The planet’s ecosystem teetered on the brink of collapse, and with it came a severe economic slump. When the disorganized leadership of the planet’s nations proved unable to turn the world back from disaster, their desperate people seized upon those who offered a chance for salvation: the United Nations. For years, the United Nations had been coordinating a mix of governments, corporations, and organizations from all over the world, sending resources from Earth to Mars. This sparked an idea. The UN assembled a plan to bring back what Earth most needed: the technological breakthroughs in terraforming developed on Mars that could be used to help restore Earth to health. It was an ambitious project, but those nations that joined saw progress and prosperity slowly return, while those that continued on their own either clung to their status quo or slipped into chaos. One by one, the nations of Earth gave up their authority to the United Nations until, out of desperation, the majority of the world followed its lead. Drawing not just upon technology but also their logistical and organizational expertise, UN technocrats reshaped the world into “Shared Interest Zones”. Often built upon former state or national boundaries, Shared Interest Zones allowed residents of an area to work toward improving their lives and the lives of their neighbors while also being a part of an effort to meet humanity’s needs wherever they were in the solar system. As the authority and operations of the United Nations grew, so did its headquarters in the Hague. Similarly, the UN’s Martian Logistics Offices in the Moon’s Lovell City were expanded and officially given what had long been their nickname: New Hague. The UN established a program called “Basic” to ensure everyone’s essential needs would be met regardless of what they chose to do with their lives. Those who did choose to do more were assigned tasks by the UN as pathways to further education, military service, or employment. Martian scientists and engineers bringing their expertise back to Earth during the early years of the UN’s projects joined teams of Earthers who volunteered to forego Basic, working together to repair the planet’s damaged ecosystem. But despite medications intended to help them adjust, Martians struggled not just with Earth’s gravity but also the growing cultural gap between Mars and Earth. The stories they told upon returning home only added to the frustrations Martians felt with Earth and the United Nations drawing away resources just as they were beginning to make progress in the Martian terraforming project.

Invoking the breakaway province rule in their charter, forty UN warships immediately set out from Earth toward Mars. Everyone was certain humanity

— Leviathan Wakes was on the brink of its first interplanetary war. To the surprise of nearly everyone, diplomacy won the day, and the warships returned to Earth, but the damage had been done; tension between the two worlds was now became a constant. As news feeds and diplomatic channels overflowed with bombast, corporations and industrial conglomerates with their own interplanetary ties tried to exert a stabilizing influence, but depleting resources exacerbated the strain. Critical elements to both worlds like lithium, molybdenum, and tungsten ran in shorter supply every year, despite deep mining into ancient landfills on Earth. Further worsening ties, the United Nations declared that all future ships were required to be built in Earth’s Bush Shipyards and that Mars’ own shipyards were to be closed. Once again, the two planets came to the brink of war. Luckily, before war could begin, humanity’s journey took its next leap forward, a leap that began in the Martian shipyards at the heart of the crisis. For years, Martian scientist Solomon Epstein had been laboring to improve starship engine efficiency. As the deadline for the shipyards’ closure approached, Epstein took the three-man yacht he outfitted with his prototype engine into orbit for a rushed test, started the burn sequence…and discovered he had succeeded beyond his wildest dreams. His yacht accelerated to speeds beyond anything previously achieved by human technology, speeds that could only be measured as a fraction of the speed of light. Tragically, the ship’s acceleration put Epstein under such intense pressure that he couldn’t lift his hand to turn the drive off. Telescopes on both Earth and Mars watched Epstein’s ship shoot toward the edges of the solar system—and then beyond. Though Epstein and his prototype were gone forever, he left the plans for what would become known as the Epstein Drive on his home computer. Knowing they couldn’t keep it secret for long, Mars instead chose to share the plans with the United Nations in exchange for independence. Mars formed its own government, the Martian Congressional Republic, and some of the first ships outfitted with the Epstein Drive were those belonging to the new Martian Congressional Republic Navy.

pages.name: The Belt and the Outer Planets

text.content:
The Epstein Drive didn’t just put Mars and Earth on more equal political and military footing, it also solved the worlds’ resource pressures by unlocking new frontiers. Scouting and science expeditions quickly ventured to most major bodies in the system; the announcements of first footsteps on yet another world soon becoming a routine feature of news feeds. But the main frontier for the first wave of expansion was the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, where increasingly rare materials on Earth or Mars could be found in abundance. Mining vessels sponsored by wealthy conglomerates were first to arrive, but eventually, smaller and smaller ships, some even home to a single family of miners, were soon to follow. Some of these prospectors struck it rich with claims that escaped the notice of the corporations, but many more endlessly traveled from rock to rock in search of that lucky strike. Soon, the asteroid belt became known as “the Belt”, and those who called it home were “Belters”. Whether large or small, every mining operation in the Belt measured their efficacy not just in what they managed to extract, but also by how they managed what their human crews needed to survive while doing so, often referred to as their “consumables”. In fact, one of the biggest success stories in the early days of the Belt wasn’t a mining operation at all, but that of Tycho Manufacturing and Engineering, which used a small fleet of ships to capture a comet as it passed through the solar system and parked it in a stable orbit within the Belt. Mining the comet’s ice, Tycho extracted both water and oxygen, resupplying Belters’ most critical consumables. Though every Belter came to Tycho’s resupply station, the company wouldn’t allow Belters to establish their own businesses in the vicinity or allow the security risk of ships docking long enough for lengthy repairs. Further, both Belter entrepreneurs and ship mechanics needed a place where they could operate in gravity that didn’t come from a ship under thrust. They had no gathering place in the Belt they could call home, so the Belters decided to build one. Eros, one of the first large asteroids to have been heavily prospected and mined, was considered but rejected when it was determined that its irregular shape made it too difficult for a pilot project. Instead of Eros, the enormous and more spherical planetoid Ceres became the chosen location. Workers turned mining shafts into an organized network of tunnels and chambers and hired Tycho to build a system of enormous reaction drives that imparted Ceres with a stable spin and gravity. It took a decade, but when the Ceres project was complete, the Belt had its first major city, and Tycho’s engineering expertise became famous throughout the system. A similar set of reaction drives were then installed to give Eros a spin, but Ceres would ever after be the mercantile center of the Belt. Instead, Eros became a center for ship manufacture and repair, as well as casinos and other entertainment facilities intended to separate crews from their money. Not long after Ceres and Eros were completed, the last of Tycho’s captured comet was broken down into consumables. But even this was to Tycho’s plan. Their facilities on the comet had been prefabricated, broken down, and moved to a new job as easily as they had been initially constructed, and the last cometary ice was sold just as prices tumbled downward. Ships that had taken colonists to establish Helium-3 refineries on the moons of Saturn were retooled to return with loads of water-ice from the near-infinite supplies in the planet’s rings. Meanwhile, Tycho’s engineers moved on to assist in another ambitious project in the outer planets: upgrades to the agricultural stations on Jupiter’s moon Ganymede. Ganymede was one of the first permanent settlements in the outer system, chosen because its magnetosphere was strong enough to shield the surface from Jupiter’s harsh radiation belts. Combined with heavy shielding, it was enough to allow crops to grow in hothouse domes on Ganymede’s surface. While small mining stations could maintain their own hydroponic gardens if they were willing to dedicate consumables to the effort, the only substantial quantities of real meat and vegetables in the outer planets came from one place—Ganymede. The same shielding that protected crops and herds also protected human embryos from genetic defects, so common wisdom in the Belt was that if you wanted to have a healthy child, you conceived and gave birth on Ganymede. These two insatiable needs—reproduction and agriculture—gave Ganymede the resources and drive it needed to enlarge and improve. Nearly every outer planet’s engineering firm, including Tycho, came to Ganymede to build new, larger domes and sets of enormous orbiting mirrors that gathered the rays of the distant sun to focus them on the domes below. A tiny outpost was then established on Titania, one of the moons of distant Uranus. An enormous and well-funded investment group contracted Tycho to design a network of colony cities that would float high in the atmosphere of the planet Venus.

As the blueprints were nearing finalization, it was revealed that certain members of the investment group lacked the authorization to allocate their funds towards off-planet development, while others possessed the necessary rights but did not have the promised financial resources. The entire group dissolved into a tangle of lawsuits and, aside from Tycho, the only group to prosper from the plan was one of the legal firms mediating the eternal dispute. Funneling their profits into shipping and interplanetary transport, the legal firm was soon dwarfed by its onetime subsidiary, Mao Mercantile, which was quickly becoming a powerhouse. Tycho, meanwhile, moved onto a new project for the Church of Latter-Day Saints: the construction of a gigantic generation ship planned for interstellar colonization.

As decades passed and whole generations were born, lived, and died in the Belt, life in microgravity made Belters taller and leaner than humans from Earth or Mars. Isolation also led Belters to develop their own language, “Belter Creole”, which incorporated words and phrases from a wide range of Earth languages along with gestures and body language easily seen while wearing a vac suit. Knit from a thousand different cloths, it was the birth of an entirely new and unique people. Although this diverse new culture came from dramatically distinct ancestries and backgrounds, there was one thing even the first Belters shared every time they got together, from gatherings on Eros to the distant docking of two prospector family ships—complaints about the Inner Planets, their corporations, and how they worked against the good of the Belt by forming the Earth-Mars Coalition. Belters extracted enormously valuable raw materials from the Belt but saw little of that wealth when it came time to sell to the Coalition. For smaller outfits, what profits they did make were almost entirely eaten up purchasing consumables like oxygen, water, and fuel they needed to survive—consumables sold by the same conglomerates buying their materials. Independence and self-reliance were core beliefs among Belters, but even the most stubborn could feel the noose tightening. If they didn’t stand together and advocate for their rights as a group, they risked becoming eternal indentured employees of the Inner Planets. From those complaints and conversations, a new group formed: the Outer Planets Alliance, otherwise known as the OPA. As anyone could declare themselves a member, the OPA had a thousand demands but no clear voice. Attempts to negotiate by regional OPA groups were often ignored by Inner Planet corporations. Events came to a head after the administrator of a distant Belt resupply station run by the Anderson-Hyosung Cooperative Industries Group increased the rates charged for consumables. These increased costs drove miners beyond the point of desperation. They gathered what aging weapons they could muster, seized control of the station, and pushed the administrator out an airlock.

He represented part of the OPA at the summit on Luna to form the Coalition to oppose the Free Navy, but, while on board the Rocinante en route back to Tycho to meet with other OPA leaders, Johnson died of a stroke during the high-g maneuvers of a battle with the Free Navy ship Pella.

In response, the United Nations sent in their Marine Corps to retake the station by force. Led by Colonel Fred Johnson and armed with cutting-edge heavy weaponry, the marines killed more than a hundred OPA insurgents and a thousand civilians in a decisive strike intended as a deterrent against future actions. Only in the aftermath was it discovered the OPA had broadcast surveillance footage from the massacre, including their surrender just before the attack began. Branded the “Butcher of Anderson Station” by the public and furious his superiors had ordered the slaughter in an attempt to cast the OPA as extremists unwilling to negotiate, Johnson resigned and publicly apologized for his role in events. Retreating to Ceres and ready to drink himself to death, Johnson was instead recruited by the OPA. Proving as apt at political strategy as he had been at military strategy, he quickly rose through its ranks to become the leader and unifying voice it had previously lacked.

A Martian scientific survey on a routine mission to explore Saturn’s moons made a landing on Phoebe. Drawing core samples to see if ice might be mined from the moon, the scientists found unexpected silicate anomalies. To investigate further, the Martian government contracted the Protogen Corporation to establish a research facility on the moon. Protogen was quick to discover answers the Martian government had kept secret, even from its trade partners—the entire moon was an extrasolar object that had arrived billions of years ago, captured by Saturn’s gravity. What’s more, deep inside the planetoid, Protogen found an adaptable set of molecular encodings able to replicate and manipulate organic matter at a molecular level. Protogen believed these would have used early life on Earth as raw materials, rebuilding and replacing it with whatever was desired by its creators. Though the origins of the planetoid and the final goals of those who sent it were a mystery, Protogen recognized the power of the tool they had discovered and gave it a name based on their own branding: the protomolecule. Protogen’s plan to investigate the power of the protomolecule was decisively ruthless. First, they trapped their Martian partner scientists in a lab on Phoebe and exposed them to the protomolecule. The experiment left no survivors. When that failed to provide enough data due to insufficient raw material for the protomolecule to transform, Protogen destroyed the station to cover their tracks, framing the OPA for the damage. Further, to spark tensions between the two planets and distract them from Protogen’s actions, they framed Mars for an attack on an Earth ship. This provided the corporation enough time to establish secret stations in outer planetary orbits, wherein they cultivated samples of the protomolecule on Eros Station in the Belt and unleashed it on the station’s population. The alien molecular machine painfully and horrifically transformed all one-and-a-half million people on the station. In charge of Tycho Station and its construction projects, the OPA tried to use the enormous bulk of the generation ship Nauvoo, which they had been constructing for the Mormons, to push Eros into the sun—only to have the station suddenly and impossibly dodge the approaching ship! In apparent defiance of everything humanity knew about thrust, momentum, and acceleration, the asteroid began moving, rapidly accelerating towards Earth. A desperate attempt to destroy Eros using Earth’s arsenal of nuclear missiles mysteriously failed when Eros somehow cloaked itself against all conventional sensors. With the entire barrage of missiles left floating aimlessly in space, the OPA seized an opportunity to retrieve them, enormously increasing the Alliance’s military might. In the end, Earth was spared because of two people: Julie Mao, a missing young woman who had been one of the protomolecule’s first victims (the “seed crystal” of its growth on Eros); and Josephus Miller, the Belter detective hired to find her. Although they were both absorbed by the protomolecule, they managed to have enough influence over it to guide Eros to crash into Venus rather than Earth. As thick clouds closed in over the impact site, the protomolecule continued its mysterious work on a planetary scale, raising crystalline towers, building vast hexagonal structures, and making flickering, ghostly lights visible to probes. Humanity was no longer alone in the Expanse.

Over a year after the Eros incident, a Martian Marine squad on Ganymede was attacked by a creature that turned out to be a Protogen engineered hybrid created using protomolecule technology. The attack and the radio blackout accompanying it set off a battle above Ganymede between UNN and MCRN ships, each side thinking the other was attacking. The sole survivor of the Martian Marine squad, Gunnery Sergeant Roberta “Bobbi” Draper, was later able to confirm the attack was caused by an outside agency. Mao-Kwikowski Mercantile, the parent corporation of Protogen, compromised members of the UN administration on Earth as part of a secret agreement to weaponize the protomolecule. Investigation of the hybrid program traced it to a secret research facility on Io. Assistant Deputy Undersecretary Chrisjen Avasarala managed to escape from temporary exile aboard a corporate-owned yacht to reach the independent ship Rocinante in attempts to alert the rest of Earth’s government to the conspiracy. Under the command of Admiral Augusto Nguyen, one of the conspirators with Protogen, UNN forces pursued Avasarala. This led to a conflict between Admiral Nguyen’s fleet, the MCR Navy, and the UNN Jupiter Fleet commanded by Admiral Michael Souther. The chaotic battle was further confused by the unclear status of the combatants. The Earth ships were hesitant to fire on each other, and the Martian ships had no idea who was on which side. Protogen’s Io facility launched a series of stealth-tech pods containing their “Caliban” hybrids towards Mars. One of the pods struck Admiral Nguyen’s command ship, the Agatha King, wherein the unleashed hybrid killed or infected most of its crew before the ship self-destructed. The remaining pods were intercepted and destroyed by allied ships and long-range missiles controlled from Tycho Station by the OPA.

Following the armistice between Earth and Mars over the Io conflict, the protomolecule constructions on the surface of Venus assembled into a massive, vaguely squid-like vessel that launched from the surface back into space. It moved approximately two astronomical units (AUs) beyond the orbit of Uranus before transforming into a massive ring some one thousand kilometers in diameter. Earth, Mars, and the OPA sent ships and observers to the newly formed Ring. Wanting to stake a claim and equal role in system affairs, the OPA sent the modified Nauvoo, rechristened as the warship Behemoth. Before the combined flotilla arrived, however, a young Belter named Menéo ‘Néo’ Yung-Espinoza accelerated a self-made racing ship, the Y Que, and shot through the Ring at high speed. He was killed instantly when the Ring activated and drastically slowed his ship—but not him. Although he didn’t live to see it, whatever Yung-Espinoze had done formed some type of wormhole inside the Ring that appeared to lead to an entirely new section of space. Seeking revenge for the ruin of her family for Protogen’s crimes, Clarissa Mao sabotaged a UN supply ship and broadcast a fake message from James Holden of the Rocinante, proclaiming OPA control of the Ring in order to frame Holden. The Behemoth fired on the Rocinante to demonstrate the OPA was not responsible. Forced to run, Holden’s ship fled through the Ring, quickly followed by several others, which were all slowed in the same way as the Y Que. The “speed limit” of what was dubbed “the Slow Zone” severely limited the ships and caused widespread injury among their crews when the ships instantly decelerated. Once inside, the Rocinante discovered an alien structure, which the crew sought to investigate. Aided by his interface with the protomolecule (which took the form of an image of the deceased Josephus Miller), Holden was able to get on board the alien control station at the center of the Slow Zone and “reset” its systems. This lifted the limits of the Slow Zone and opened more than 1300 other gates within it, leading to other star systems. It also offered Holden a vision of the control station directing energy through some of those gates to destroy entire systems, a scorched earth tactic intended to stop…something, perhaps the threat that exterminated the mysterious Builders of the protomolecule and the Slow Zone. Subsequently, the OPA parked the Behemoth in the Slow Zone in orbit of the control station, renaming it Medina Station, and securing their involvement in the control of the gates. The wider galaxy beyond the reaches of the solar system was open to humanity for the very first time.

Explorers, prospectors, and would-be colonists rushed through the Ring gates into the systems beyond. In spite of the best efforts of the UN, Mars, and the OPA to try and manage the chaos, humanity would no longer be contained. The human need to explore and expand (and to seek profit and opportunity) drove people outwards. By the time the Inner Planets and the OPA could even begin to get a handle on things, it was already too late. Explorers discovered many of the systems connected by the Ring gates had Earth-like planets, worlds where the native life had been repurposed by the protomolecule to create their Rings, but while they often found surprisingly intact ruins or other artifacts, there was no evidence at all of the mysterious Builders— other than that they had clearly been gone for billions of years. Nevertheless, they built to last, and, like the Ring network itself, some of their technology was still functional, offering untold opportunities— and dangers—for explorers. Under Duarte’s command, the Martian expatriates transited to the system they named Laconia, where they set up a military state on the terrestrial planet. Winston Duarte declared himself “First Consul” of Laconia, its absolute ruler, and closed off the system, promising to destroy any ship that transits its gate. So it has remained since the end of the Free Navy Conflict, but Winston Duarte’s plans—for Laconia, the Ring system, and humanity—have only just begun.

colonists removed from “their” planet. The UN designated the planet “New Terra” and sent the crew of the Rocinante to help negotiate. The conflict escalated to violence, which came to a sudden and destructive conclusion when an ancient fusion reactor on the planet went super-critical. The ensuing explosion sent a shockwave and tsunami that destroyed the colony while triggering some sort of Builder failsafe technology, which suppressed all nuclear fusion on the planet and in orbit, shutting down ships and causing their orbits to decay. Some of the colonists survived by taking shelter in ancient Builder ruins. Just like on the Ring station, Captain Holden eventually managed to access the Builder technology on the planet and reset it. Following the devastation, an exploration of the Builder ruins on Illus revealed further evidence that some outside force had destroyed the Builders, and that the reactivation of their technology might begin drawing their notice. While the diaspora through the Ring gates allowed for many who felt they led otherwise meaningless lives on Earth to leave the system to become colonists or explorers, it had far more serious implications for Mars and the Belt. With the promise of a thousand or more Earth-like worlds to settle, the urgency of Mars’ “great endeavor” became far less. Why take part in a terraforming project that wouldn’t be complete in your lifetime when you could colonize a new, living world now? Martians abandoned their world in increasing numbers, their skills in high demand. Likewise, the promise of those new systems offered planets with resources that could be exploited by people living down a gravity well—where the Belters could not survive. They suddenly found themselves facing obsolescence, no longer even valuable to the Inners as cheap resource-mining labor.

Immediately seeing the impact of the opening of the Ring gates on the future of Mars, Winston Duarte of the MCRN began secretly organizing a contingency plan for his people and humanity. As with the discovery of the protomolecule, Martian explorers discovered a system through one of the Ring gates where a Builder construction platform still existed in orbit of the terrestrial planet. A logistics manager, Duarte buried reports about the system and began quietly reshuffling resources behind the scenes, recruiting additional Martian military personnel. He subtly contacted the most radical factions of the OPA and began delivering Martian weapons, ships, and resources into their hands, and he arranged for the theft of the only known remaining sample of the protomolecule in the Sol system from Tycho Station. Emboldened and empowered by their secret alliance with Duarte, the radical OPA factions, led by Marco Inaros, planned a secret offensive against the Inner Planets and the non-aligned elements of the Outer Planets Alliance. Stealing Martian stealth technology, they used it to conceal a series of small asteroids and changed their orbits to collide with Earth. They set up an ambush to capture or assassinate the Martian Prime Minister, and they arranged coups on board Tycho Station and on Medina Station to seize control of the Slow Zone and the Ring network. Although Prime Minister Nathan Smith survived due to the last-minute intervention of Bobbi Draper and Alex Kamal, and the Tycho Station coup was ultimately thwarted, the other offensives were successful: Earth was devastated by a series of three asteroid strikes, and Medina Station fell under the control of what Inaros called “the Free Navy” of the Belt.
